title: Bayesian Financial Portfolio Analysis in R
text:
Preface
This is a tutorial of Bayesian analysis financial applications by R machinery. Some key financial concepts can be worked with Bayesian theory. I can’t say anything of stock trading without effort, it’s a risky business. Things can go wrong, data aren’t obtained correctly. But a correct set of prior beliefs can certainly help.
To learn more about Quarto books visit https://quarto.org/docs/books.

title: 1  Bayesian Portfolio Posterior Return and Risk
text:
For stocks, the stock returns are assumed to be normally distributed with a mean return vector and a covariance matrix. A portfolio is simply a weight vector tells us to allocate assets. Portfolio return is a weighted sum, portfolio risk is a quadratic form.
From the assumption, we can obtain posterior mean return vectors and posterior covariance matrices for the stock returns.

Coderm(list=ls(all=TRUE))

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(rjags)
library(tidybayes)
library(xts)
library(SharpeR)# data

data(stock_returns)
r<-stock_returns
head(r)

                    IBM        AAPL          SPY          XOM
2000-01-04 -0.034533362 -0.08807784 -0.039891663 -0.019339627
2000-01-05  0.034533362  0.01452826  0.001787736  0.053081564
2000-01-06 -0.017391710 -0.09051434 -0.016201978  0.050405613
2000-01-07 -0.004395653  0.04628092  0.056452003 -0.002938958
2000-01-10  0.038881562 -0.01774458  0.003425019 -0.014079528
2000-01-11  0.008439341 -0.05250528 -0.012038322  0.002980649

CodeN=nrow(r)
K=4
set.seed(123)

model_code <- "
model {
  #likelihood
  for (i in 1:N) {
    y[i,] ~ dmnorm(mu, Sigma_Inv)
  }

  # Prior on mean vector
  for(k in 1:K) {
    mu[k]~dnorm(0, 1 /100 ^ 2)
  }

  # Prior on covariance matrix
  Sigma_Inv ~ dwish(I, K+1)
}
"
data_list <- list(
  N = N,
  K=K,
  I = diag(K),
  y=r
)
model <- jags.model(textConnection(model_code), 
                    data=data_list, 
                    n.chains = 5);

Compiling model graph
   Resolving undeclared variables
   Allocating nodes
Graph information:
   Observed stochastic nodes: 4777
   Unobserved stochastic nodes: 5
   Total graph size: 4809

Initializing model

Codeupdate(model, 1000, progress.bar = "none"); # Burnin for 1000 samples

posterior_sample <- coda.samples(model, 
                                 variable.names = c("mu","Sigma_Inv"),
                                 n.iter = 10, progress.bar = "none")

#summary(posterior_sample)

mu_dat <-         posterior_sample %>% spread_draws(mu[i]|i)#tidybayes
Sigma_Inv_dat <- posterior_sample %>%  tidy_draws(Sigma_Inv)#tidybayes


With a known portfolio vector, the posterior portfolio return Figure 1.1 is a weighted sum of posterior stock mean returns. The posterior portfolio risk Figure 1.2 is a quadratic form of posterior return covariance matrices.

Code#portfolio return posterior distribution
port=c(0.20247656,  0.26518714, 0.3566089,  0.17572744)

er=as.matrix(mu_dat[,4:7])
port.return=er%*%port
plot(density(port.return),lwd=4,col=4,main="Porsterior Return Distribution")






Figure 1.1: Posterior Portfolio Return Distribution





Code#portfolio risk posterior distribution
port.risk=NULL
for(i in 1:nrow(Sigma_Inv_dat)){
  covmat = solve(matrix(as.numeric(Sigma_Inv_dat[i,4:19]),ncol=4))
  port.risk=c(port.risk,port%*%covmat%*%port)
}
plot(density(port.risk),lwd=4,col=4,main="Posterior Risk Distribution")






Figure 1.2: Posterior Portfolio Risk Distribution

title: 2  Bayesian Posterior Portfolio Frontier
text:
It was in our financial theory classes, we were introduced to portfolio frontier and optimized portfolio, especially the minimum risk portfolio. But when we applied the theory from class the minimum risk portfolio was not minimum risk at all.
Think about it in the real world, every time we want to do something a new set of data are deliver to us. Only look at one set of data or one frontier is insufficient. Luckily rJAGS can help us to simulate the full set of posterior distribution of frontiers. We can have an overall view of the portfolio optimization problem.
We first load the data, and compute the direct estimated portfolio frontier.

Coderm(list=ls(all=TRUE))

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(rjags)
library(tidybayes)
library(IntroCompFinR )
library(xts)
library(SharpeR)# data

data(stock_returns)
r<-stock_returns
head(r)

                    IBM        AAPL          SPY          XOM
2000-01-04 -0.034533362 -0.08807784 -0.039891663 -0.019339627
2000-01-05  0.034533362  0.01452826  0.001787736  0.053081564
2000-01-06 -0.017391710 -0.09051434 -0.016201978  0.050405613
2000-01-07 -0.004395653  0.04628092  0.056452003 -0.002938958
2000-01-10  0.038881562 -0.01774458  0.003425019 -0.014079528
2000-01-11  0.008439341 -0.05250528 -0.012038322  0.002980649

CodeN=nrow(r)
K=4
set.seed(123)

#Direct estimation
Er=colMeans(r)
S=cov(r)

ef <- efficient.frontier(Er, S, alpha.min=-2,
                         alpha.max=1.5, nport=20)
y= ef$er
x= ef$sd


We generate posterior distribution of returns and covariance matrix.

Codemodel_code <- "
model {
  #likelihood
  for (i in 1:N) {
    y[i,] ~ dmnorm(mu, Sigma_Inv)
  }
  for(k in 1:K) {
    mu[k]~dnorm(0, 1 /100 ^ 2)
  }

  # Prior on covariance matrix
  Sigma_Inv ~ dwish(I, K+1)
}
"
data_list <- list(
  N = N,
  K=K,
  I = diag(K),
  y=r
)
model <- jags.model(textConnection(model_code), 
                    data=data_list, 
                    n.chains = 5);

Compiling model graph
   Resolving undeclared variables
   Allocating nodes
Graph information:
   Observed stochastic nodes: 4777
   Unobserved stochastic nodes: 5
   Total graph size: 4809

Initializing model

Codeupdate(model, 1000, progress.bar = "none"); # Burnin for 1000 samples

posterior_sample <- coda.samples(model, 
                                 variable.names = c("mu","Sigma_Inv"),
                                 n.iter = 10, progress.bar = "none")

#summary(posterior_sample)

mu_dat <-         posterior_sample %>% spread_draws(mu[i]|i)#tidybayes
Sigma_Inv_dat <- posterior_sample %>%  tidy_draws(Sigma_Inv)#tidybayes


Construct all frontiers from the posterior distribution.

Code#Posterior frontiers
efr=NULL
efs=NULL
n=nrow(mu_dat)
m=20
for(i in 1:n){
  er =as.numeric(mu_dat[i,4:7])
  covmat = solve(matrix(as.numeric(Sigma_Inv_dat[i,4:19]),ncol=4))

  # compute portfolio frontier
  ef <- efficient.frontier(er, covmat, alpha.min=-2,
                         alpha.max=1.5, nport=m)
 efr=c(efr, ef$er)
 efs=c(efs, ef$sd)
}


Plot the posterior frontiers.

Codeggplot() +
  # Plot posterior sample densities
  geom_path(
    aes(x = efs, y = efr,group = rep(1:n, each = m),linetype = "Posterior frontiers" ),
    color = "gray",
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
 
  # Plot posterior expected density
  geom_path(
    aes(x = x, y =y,linetype = "Direct estimated frontier" ),
    color = "black"
  ) + labs(linetype ="")+ #"Reference Lines"

  # Labels and theme
  labs(
    x = "Risk",
    y = "Expected Return"
  )+theme(legend.position = "top")






Figure 2.1: Posterior frontier Distribution




Figure 2.1 The minimum risk portfolio from direct estimation (black curve) has daily return around 0.00025. But our posterior frontiers show that many minimum risk portfolios have daily return less than 0.00025 or lower than zero. We cannot reject Hypothesis that minimum risk portfolio return is less than 0.

title: 3  Black-Litterman Posterior Predictive
text:
Say there are 4 stocks, their daily returns are assumed to be normally distributed with means and a covariance matrix. If someone tell us, there was one day the stocks had a portfolio gained such such return. Should we believe it?
Let’s say the portfolio was \((0.20247656,  0.26518714, 0.3566089,  0.17572744)\), and the portfolio return on that day was \(0.01016\). Black-Litterman model says with a known risk free rate and covariance matrix we can compute the stock returns used. We load the data.

Coderm(list=ls(all=TRUE))
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(rjags)
library(tidybayes)
library(xts)
library(SharpeR)# data
library(gridExtra)

data(stock_returns)
r<-stock_returns
head(r)

                    IBM        AAPL          SPY          XOM
2000-01-04 -0.034533362 -0.08807784 -0.039891663 -0.019339627
2000-01-05  0.034533362  0.01452826  0.001787736  0.053081564
2000-01-06 -0.017391710 -0.09051434 -0.016201978  0.050405613
2000-01-07 -0.004395653  0.04628092  0.056452003 -0.002938958
2000-01-10  0.038881562 -0.01774458  0.003425019 -0.014079528
2000-01-11  0.008439341 -0.05250528 -0.012038322  0.002980649

CodeN=nrow(r)
K=4


Use rJAGS to get posterior distributions of the returns.

Codeset.seed(123)

model_code <- "
model {
  #likelihood
  for (i in 1:N) {
    y[i,] ~ dmnorm(mu, Sigma_Inv)
  }

  # Prior on mean vector
  for(k in 1:K) {
    mu[k]~dnorm(0, 1 /100 ^ 2)
  }

  # Prior on covariance matrix
  Sigma_Inv ~ dwish(I, K+1)
}
"
data_list <- list(
  N = N,
  K=K,
  I = diag(K),
  y=r
)
model <- jags.model(textConnection(model_code), 
                    data=data_list, 
                    n.chains = 5);

Compiling model graph
   Resolving undeclared variables
   Allocating nodes
Graph information:
   Observed stochastic nodes: 4777
   Unobserved stochastic nodes: 5
   Total graph size: 4809

Initializing model

Codeupdate(model, 1000, progress.bar = "none"); # Burnin for 1000 samples

posterior_sample <- coda.samples(model, 
                                 variable.names = c("mu","Sigma_Inv"),
                                 n.iter = 10, progress.bar = "none")

#summary(posterior_sample)

mu_dat <-         posterior_sample %>% spread_draws(mu[i]|i)#tidybayes
Sigma_Inv_dat <- posterior_sample %>%  tidy_draws(Sigma_Inv)#tidybayes


Let \(x\) be the portfolio vector, \(r_x\) be portfolio return, \(r_f\) be risk-free-rate, \(S\) be covariance matrix of the stock returns. We have: \[\lambda=\frac{r_x-r_f}{x^TSx}\] Let \(r\) be computed stock returns: \[r=\lambda Sx+r_f\]

Code#Black-Litterman Model
S=cov(r)
risk.free.rate=.01 #risk free rate
port=c(0.20247656,  0.26518714, 0.3566089,  0.17572744)#envelope portfolio
port.r=0.01016 #portfolio reurn
var_port=port%*%S%*%port
lambda=as.numeric((port.r-risk.free.rate)/var_port)
implied.r=lambda*S%*%port+risk.free.rate
implied.r

           [,1]
IBM  0.01013725
AAPL 0.01025938
SPY  0.01012222
XOM  0.01011292


We plot computed returns against posterior return distributions. We can see the computed returns are very far away from posterior return distributions. We can conclude to get such high return from the stocks was not plausible.

Code#posterior predictive plot

posterior_ret <- rename_with(mu_dat, function(x) paste0("Posterior_return_", x))#dplyr
names(posterior_ret)

[1] "Posterior_return_.chain"     "Posterior_return_.iteration"
[3] "Posterior_return_.draw"      "Posterior_return_1"         
[5] "Posterior_return_2"          "Posterior_return_3"         
[7] "Posterior_return_4"         

Code# Density curves
p1<-ggplot(posterior_ret, aes(x=Posterior_return_1)) + geom_density(alpha=.5)+
    geom_vline(aes(xintercept=mean(implied.r[1,1], na.rm=T)),   
               color="red", linetype="dashed", size=1)
p2<-ggplot(posterior_ret, aes(x=Posterior_return_2)) + geom_density(alpha=.5)+
    geom_vline(aes(xintercept=mean(implied.r[1,1], na.rm=T)),   
               color="red", linetype="dashed", size=1)
p3<-ggplot(posterior_ret, aes(x=Posterior_return_3)) + geom_density(alpha=.5)+
    geom_vline(aes(xintercept=mean(implied.r[1,1], na.rm=T)),   
               color="red", linetype="dashed", size=1)
p4<-ggplot(posterior_ret, aes(x=Posterior_return_4)) + geom_density(alpha=.5)+
    geom_vline(aes(xintercept=mean(implied.r[1,1], na.rm=T)),   
               color="red", linetype="dashed", size=1)

grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, p4, ncol = 2)

title: 4  Bayesian Optimization Pairs Trading
text:
https://zorro-project.com/manual/en/Lecture%204.htm
Pairs trading, hedge ratio we knew them, no need to repeat anything. Again I adopted codes from link above. You may want to read it from there. For pairs trading we need an upper bond and a lower bond to mark entry points for placing orders, the bonds can be computed as \(mean \pm sdtv\). In this material we have optimized bonds are \((-0.02238346,  8.56827139)\). Let’s make a plot with the optimized bonds Figure 4.1.

Coderequire(quantmod)
require(PerformanceAnalytics)
require(rBayesianOptimization)


rm(list=ls(all=TRUE))
set.seed(4587)
setwd("C:\\tuDrive2026\\Bayesian-Financial-Portfolio-Analysis-in-R\\")

QQQQ<-read.csv("QQQQ.csv")

Code BB   <- mydata$X601857.Close
 QQ   <- mydata$X601318.Close
 
 #define training set
 rangeT  <-mydata[,1]
 BB   <- as.ts(BB)
 QQ   <- as.ts(QQ)

#compute price differences on in-sample data
 pdBB <- diff(BB)[-1]
 pdQQ <- diff(QQ)[-1]
 
 #build the model
 model  <- lm(pdBB ~ pdQQ - 1)

 #extract the hedge ratio
 hr     <- as.numeric(model$coefficients[1])

#spread price (in-sample)
 spreadT <- BB - hr * QQ
 
 #compute statistics of the spread
 meanT    <- as.numeric(mean(spreadT,na.rm=TRUE))
 sdT      <- as.numeric(sd(spreadT,na.rm=TRUE))
 upperThr <- 8.56827139
 lowerThr <- -0.02238346



Code #visualize the in-sample spread + stats
 plot(spreadT, main = "AAPL vs. QQQ spread (in-sample period)")
 abline(h = meanT, col = "red", lwd =2)
 abline(h = upperThr, col = "blue", lwd=2)
 abline(h = lowerThr, col = "blue", lwd=2)






Figure 4.1: Plot upper and lower thresholds with residual series.




The code below shows to buy and sell with the thresholds and the residual series Figure 4.2. The logic is nice and clear, no need to say much about it.

CodeindSell <- which(spreadT >= upperThr)
indBuy  <- which(spreadT <= lowerThr)

 spreadL  <- length(spreadT)
 pricesB  <- c(rep(NA,spreadL))
 pricesS  <- c(rep(NA,spreadL))
 sp       <- as.numeric(spreadT)
 tradeQty <- 100
 totalP   <- 0
 holding.pos<-length(spreadT)

 for(i in 1:spreadL) {
     spTemp <- sp[i]
     if(spTemp < lowerThr) {
        if(totalP <= 0){ #have some to buy
           totalP     <- totalP + tradeQty
           pricesB[i] <- spTemp
        }
     } else if(spTemp > upperThr) {
       if(totalP >= 0){ #have some to sell
          totalP <- totalP - tradeQty
          pricesS[i] <- spTemp
       }
    }
  holding.pos[i]<-totalP
 }


 plot(spreadT, main = "BBBB vs. QQQQ spread (in-sample period)")
 abline(h = meanT, col = "red", lwd =2)
 abline(h = upperThr, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
 abline(h = lowerThr, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
 points(as.ts(pricesB,index(spreadT)), col="green", cex=1.9, pch=19)#buy
 points(as.ts(pricesS,index(spreadT)), col="red", cex=1.9, pch=19)#sell


spReturns = diff(sp)/tail(sp,-1)#lagged
trading.sign=sign(tail(holding.pos,-1))#lagged

trading.return=trading.sign*spReturns 
sum(trading.return)

Figure 4.2: Two order entry points red and green




After we can place orders, we can compute return series of the orders, also use Sharpe ratio to evaluate the return series. The upper lower thresholds which produce the best Sharpe ratio for our residuals series are the best thresholds. Optimization method we using here is Bayesian optimization. The end result is what we used for plotting.

Codeopt_thresholds <- function(lower, upper) {
 lowerThr=lower
 upperThr=upper
 spreadL  <- length(spreadT)

 sp       <- as.numeric(spreadT)
 tradeQty <- 100
 totalP   <- 0
 holding.pos<-length(spreadT)

 for(i in 1:spreadL) {
     spTemp <- sp[i]
     if(spTemp < lowerThr) {
        if(totalP <= 0){ #have some to buy
           totalP     <- totalP + tradeQty
            }
     } else if(spTemp > upperThr) {
       if(totalP >= 0){ #have some to sell
          totalP <- totalP - tradeQty
           }
    }
  holding.pos[i]<-totalP
 }
spReturns = diff(sp)/tail(sp,-1)#lagged
trading.sign=sign(tail(holding.pos,-1))#lagged

trading.return=trading.sign*spReturns 

sr=SharpeRatio(as.ts(trading.return), Rf=.035/252, FUN="StdDev") #252 tradings a year
return(list(Score = as.numeric(sr[,1])))# returns a score list

}

# Bayesian Optimization
optimizer <- BayesianOptimization(
  FUN = opt_thresholds,
  bounds = list(lower = c(-2, 0), upper = c(.01, 19)),
  init_points = 10,
  n_iter = 10,
  acq = "ucb",
  verbose = TRUE
)

title: 5  Hilbert Space Approximated Price Prediction
text:
https://juanitorduz.github.io/hsgp_intro/
I don’t want to go over any math but to keep very thing simple. If you want to have a more detailed introduction you can read materials from link above. The data I use I have uploaded them to github repo. After loaded the data I just take 30 data points, use 20 data points in the middle for model building, first 5 data points to test back casting, and last 5 data points to test forecasting. The price data are logged, but for analysis I will use exponential function to get them back as showing on plotting.

The \(phi\) matrix does not depend on the data, it needs to be imported into JAG. For model building, the simple formulas are from the link above. I just let JAG outputs some predictions collect them for analysis.

Codem=20 
L=2

phi=sqrt(1/L)*sin(outer(x+L,pi*1:m,"*")/2/L)

gp_model <- '
model{

  for(i in 1:m){
    S[i]=a^2*sqrt(2*pi)*l^1*exp(-.5*l^2*((i)*pi/2/L)^2)
    beta[i] ~ dnorm(0,1);
  }

  gp <- phi %*% (sqrt(S)*beta );

  for(i in 6:25){
    y[i]~dnorm(gp[i],sigma_y^-2);

  }
  for(i in 1:n){
    y_pred[i]~dnorm(gp[i],sigma_y^-2);
  }
  a ~ dgamma(a1,b1)#amplitude 
  l ~ dgamma(a2,b2)#length_scale
  sigma_y ~  dt(0,10^-2,1)T(0,)#error term 

}'


data_list<-list(y = y, pi = pi, m = m, L=L,
                a1=8, b1=5, a2=1, b2=1,
                phi=phi,n=n)
                  
##parameters to save
jags_pars <- c("y_pred") #
 
model <- jags.model(textConnection(gp_model), data=data_list, n.chains = 5)

As we see Figure 5.1, data points on left-hand-side of blue vertical line are for test back casting, data points on right-hand-side of orange vertical line are for test forecasting. The blue band is 95% confidence interval for prediction. The confidence interval does not cover testing data properly, and the interval is too wide. We may want to use the model to predict stock returns which are more likely to be normally distributed.
